title: Europeans Should Learn to Love the Air-Conditioner

vocab.articleQuote: judiciously dialling down the temperature will not do much to melt the glaciers.
vocab.inContext: Used as the adverb "judiciously," it means cooling a home thoughtfully and in moderation — only as much as you actually need — rather than blasting the AC carelessly, so the extra emissions stay small.
vocab.meaning: Showing good, careful judgment; sensible and well-considered in the decisions you make.
examples: She made a judicious choice to study a little each night instead of cramming the evening before the exam.
A judicious coach rests the star player once the game is already won, saving her for the playoffs.

vocab.articleQuote: Italy is a laggard, getting 30-40% of its electricity from gas.
vocab.inContext: Italy is falling behind other European countries on clean energy because it still leans heavily on gas to make electricity.
vocab.meaning: A person, group, or thing that moves or progresses more slowly than the rest — one that lags behind.
examples: Once the laggard of the league, the team finally climbed out of last place this season.
He was the laggard of the group hike, always trailing a few minutes behind everyone else.

vocab.articleQuote: Yanks holidaying in Europe expect cool comfort, and grow surly on finding that many old-world buildings require them to sweat and bear it.
vocab.inContext: American tourists turn bad-tempered and grumpy when they discover that European buildings often have no air-conditioning.
vocab.meaning: Bad-tempered, sullen, and unfriendly in the way you speak or act.
examples: The surly cashier barely looked up and grunted when I asked where the milk was.
He gets surly when he's hungry, snapping at everyone until he's finally had lunch.

vocab.articleQuote: And astute governments offer funding to make old houses energy-efficient, which can pay for itself.
vocab.inContext: Smart, sharp-thinking governments recognize that paying to upgrade old houses now will save money on energy later.
vocab.meaning: Having or showing a clever, sharp understanding of a situation; shrewd and perceptive.
examples: An astute shopper compares the price per ounce instead of just the number on the sticker.
She made an astute observation that the movie's villain had been hinted at in the very first scene.

vocab.articleQuote: But its 224g of CO2 per kilowatt-hour is positively verdant next to much of America.
vocab.inContext: The writer is punning on the word: Italy's electricity is environmentally "green" (clean) compared with America's, even though it is far from perfect.
vocab.meaning: Literally, green and lush with growing plants; often used figuratively to mean "green" in the environmental, eco-friendly sense.
examples: After the spring rains, the once-brown hills turned verdant almost overnight.
The valley below us was a verdant patchwork of rice paddies and tea gardens.

vocab.articleQuote: Europe's southerners think coddled Americans don't know how to cope with heat naturally.
vocab.inContext: Southern Europeans see Americans as pampered and over-comforted by constant air-conditioning, so they've never learned to handle heat on their own.
vocab.meaning: Treated with excessive care and protection; pampered. To coddle someone is to baby them.
examples: He complained that his little brother was coddled — never made to do chores or face any consequences.
Some say young athletes are coddled with constant praise and never learn to handle criticism.

quiz.question: What is the article's main reason that Europeans shouldn't feel guilty about using more air-conditioning?
options: Air-conditioners have become much cheaper to buy than before
Much of Europe's electricity now comes from clean sources like solar, nuclear, and hydro, so the extra emissions are small
Climate change has already been solved, so emissions no longer matter
Europeans use far less electricity overall than they did a decade ago
quiz.explanation: The article's central point is that Europe's increasingly clean electricity mix means running the AC adds relatively little CO2.

quiz.question: The article says a kilowatt-hour of electricity in Spain produced far less CO2 (86g) than one in the U.S. state of Georgia (442g). What mainly explains that gap?
options: Spain's homes are larger than Georgia's
Spain measures its emissions in a different unit
The mix of energy sources used to generate it — Spain leans on solar, while Georgia burns more fossil fuels
Georgia actually uses more solar power than Spain does
quiz.explanation: The same kilowatt-hour is "cleaner" or "dirtier" depending on what generated it; Spain's solar-heavy grid emits far less than a fossil-fuel-heavy one.

quiz.question: To "judiciously" dial down the temperature means to do it...
options: carelessly and without much thought
with good judgment and in moderation
only when guests are visiting
as a last resort, very reluctantly
quiz.explanation: Judicious means showing careful, sensible judgment — here, cooling only as much as you actually need.

quiz.question: When the article calls Italy "a laggard" on clean energy, it means Italy is...
options: a leader that other countries try to copy
one that falls behind the others
a country with no fossil fuels at all
the cleanest performer in the group
quiz.explanation: A laggard is one that lags behind the rest; Italy trails because it still relies heavily on gas.

quiz.question: Which word from the reading means "shrewd and sharp in understanding a situation"?
options: surly
verdant
astute
coddled
quiz.explanation: Astute means perceptive and clever; the article praises "astute governments" for funding efficiency upgrades that pay for themselves.
